steps.text: In a real game nobody tells you which piece to think about, and the board is full. You already know how a rook slides. This lesson is about reading a crowded board without mistakes. First watch one worked example, then try a quiet board yourself.

steps.caption: A busier board. The white rook is on d4. Walk outward from it, one direction at a time, and stop at the first piece you meet.

claims.statement: The piece on d4 is a white rook.

steps.caption: Up. d5 is empty, then White's own pawn stands on d6.

line.say: The rook may stop on d5. Its own pawn on d6 is the first piece, so d6 and beyond are closed.

claims.statement: The rook can go to d5.
The rook cannot land on its own pawn.
The rook cannot jump the pawn.

steps.caption: Down. Nothing stands on d3, d2 or d1.

line.say: Three empty squares and then the edge: the rook can stop on any of them, even the last.

claims.statement: The rook can go to d3.
The rook can go to d1.

steps.caption: Left. c4 is empty, then a black knight stands on b4.

line.say: The first piece is an enemy knight, so the rook may take it. The slide ends there, and a4 is out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook can go to c4.
The rook can take on b4.
The rook cannot go past the knight to a4.
A black knight stands on b4.

steps.caption: Right. e4 and f4 are empty, then White's own pawn stands on g4.

line.say: Two free squares. The rook stops on f4, one short of its own pawn. h4 behind the pawn is closed.

claims.statement: The rook can go to f4.
The rook cannot land on its own pawn.
The rook cannot jump the pawn.

steps.caption: All together: eight squares. One up, three down, two left (one of them a capture), two right. The bishop on e5 and the pawns on g7 and h7 are on none of the rook's lines, so they change nothing.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on d4 can move to.

steps.caption: For comparison, the same rook on an empty board reaches fourteen squares. Every blocker on a line removes squares, so a busy board gives a smaller number.

claims.statement: On an empty board the rook on d4 reaches exactly these fourteen squares.

steps.text: **Three questions, in this order.** What piece is it? Which lines does it travel on? What is the first piece on each line: nothing, one of yours, or an enemy? A piece standing on a line is a **blocker**. [I] Walking outward line by line probably works better than scanning the whole board, because each line ends at its first piece.
Nobody will tell you the piece is a rook. A different piece takes a different walk, so name the piece before you draw a single line. Here is the same board again, with other pieces on d4.

steps.caption: A bishop on d4. It travels on diagonals, so the squares it reaches are not the rook's squares at all. Its own bishop on e5 closes one diagonal at once.

line.say: Up and to the left along the diagonal to the edge: three squares, a move no rook can make.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the bishop on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white bishop.

steps.caption: A knight on d4. It jumps in an L, and jumping ignores blockers. Eight squares, and not one is on the rook's lines.

line.say: The knight leaps two squares up and one across. What stands in between does not matter.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the knight on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white knight.

steps.caption: A queen on d4 does both jobs: all the rook's squares and all the bishop's squares, fifteen in total here. Name the piece and you know which lines to walk.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white queen.

steps.text: **Remember.** A rook slides straight along its lines. Name the piece first, then walk outward one direction at a time and stop at the first piece you meet. Your own piece stops you one square short. An enemy piece can be captured. Every blocker removes squares, so a busy board gives a smaller number.
